text: Rockridge retail vitality is holding at 12.22, yet sentiment registers at 0.02 against the citywide 0.107 mark, demonstrating persistent operational friction that solid corridor foot traffic alone cannot resolve. Following the contained fire in KONO, municipal follow-through must center on disciplined structural code inspections and tracking emergency costs rather than unmonitored off-budget allocations. In District 7, we verify ground conditions before deploying resources, while ensuring Temescal Community Health Center continues delivering under its remaining $15,576,923.05 operational budget.

Procedural integrity requires that every council action rests on an official roll call and verifiable docket records. District 8 continues to insist on Chen-Vega audit controls for Grand Lake commercial stabilization, while demanding transparent departmental coordination to reconcile municipal service delivery and health readings across Eastlake and Adams Point.

I am holding Baylight District — Final Council Vote this week. The board marks it complete and schedules no next action, so I see no basis for another work move. Jack London’s sentiment is positive and its crime index is below the city figure, though retail vitality eased; Baylight District is still marked as declining. I want to review implementation outcomes before considering any further step, rather than treating completion as proof of a particular neighborhood result.

**Cycle 116 weekly report — Marcus Webb, OEWD Program Director, West Oakland Stabilization Fund (INIT-001)**

**Where the money stands.** The Fund's authorization is $28 million; the tracker shows $20.6 million remaining as of this Cycle. The last recorded disbursement was Cycle 116 under the standing 23-day processing standard. I'm not going to quote a cumulative number beyond what the sheet supports: the payments record carries one row total, and the tracker's tranche lines are the authority for the rest. The four household grants I can name on the record — HH-0102-F027, HH-0109-F017, HH-0110-F019, HH-0113-F023, all West Oakland renters — are active, last paid between Cycles 109 and 113, no flags.

**The queue.** No new payment lines this Cycle. That is the part I answer for plainly: the clock held on what was already in motion, but nothing new went out the door in Cycle 116. Next cycle's opening task is the same as this cycle's closing one — get the next authorization batch in front of the Deputy Mayor's desk, not a memo about it.

**The charter renewal.** The ordinance is on the Council calendar. The closeout from Cycle 114 is published, the business-and-resident scope is preserved exactly as corrected in C109, and the 23-day standard is written into the conditions. Final action is set for Cycle 117. I want to be clear about the two things the press has rightly pressed on: the scope did move twice on the record (C108 then C109), and that history is now part of the hearing record rather than a footnote — and the renewal vote is the Council's to cast, not mine to predict. What I control is the proof, and the proof is published.

**The neighborhoods.** West Oakland's housing pressure reads 5.5 this Cycle with a median rent of $3,669 and a trajectory of growth. That is the pressure the Fund exists to answer, and it is the reason the queue cannot idle while paperwork moves. I'm also noting the tenant-defense sequencing decision on the record this Cycle: the legal-support record goes first, and the 23-day clock runs while it does — the rent doesn't wait for an ordinance.

**What I'm watching.** The Council roll call in 117. Before it, verified closeout, verified scope, verified clock — all three on the hearing record. After it, execution on Day One of whatever the Council decides.

**Weekly Report — Cycle 116. Elena Soria Dominguez, Transit Hub Planning Lead.**

Here's what's on the record this week, and here's what actually changed.

**Fruitvale.** The hub's visioning phase is complete and it's showing where it counts: 9,343 riders this cycle, up from 8,943 — a 4.5% gain — with the best on-time performance of any station in the system at 0.83. No BART train events on the sheet. No payments out on INIT-003 this cycle. So I want to be clear with the Mayor and the council: the numbers moved, but nothing was built. That's ridership following life, not a drawing.

**The rest of the system.** On-time performance came down citywide — 12th Street 0.86 to 0.81, 19th Street 0.81 to 0.78, Lake Merritt 0.83 to 0.77. 12th Street lost 2,313 riders and 19th Street 2,251. I told this room in an earlier cycle not to hang that on the hub, and I'll say it again, though this week I'd note it plainly: game-day crowds through Jack London and Downtown, crowded platforms, and a gridlock day �� traffic index 79, worst on I-880 South. My East Oakland stations, Fruitvale and Coliseum, both held at 0.83. That's not a coincidence I'm claiming; it's what the sheet says.

**Roads.** Every corridor improved against the prior cycle — I-880 North 100 to 89, I-880 South 98 to 92, I-980 100 to 86, Broadway 85 to 72, International 84 to 73. Heavy congestion remains, but the direction is right, and International Blvd — the corridor my neighbors actually walk and cross — moved from heavy to moderate. Event traffic from the Oaks home week is in the record on top of that.

**Infrastructure.** A medium-severity public-works spike in Glenview and a stalled bus in East Oakland. Neither on my docket, both on my radar, and neither acceptable to shrug at.

**Where the project stands.** Closure isn't decision. The schematics delivery and the documented Fruitvale community review are directed, and further design advancement waits on a public comment-and-response record that does not yet exist. Merchant covenants are executed and Mayer & Associates is under contract with community oversight provisions. Doña Esperanza's cart is in those drawings. I intend it to stay there when they're real.

That's my report. It's on the record as given.

**Cycle 116 — Weekly Report on the Record**
**Keisha Ramos, Director, Baylight Authority**

INIT-006 status: unchanged, and I want that said plainly before anything else. The C115 evidence-file review is closed. No construction milestone has been declared passed. The tracker still reads "remediation, hotline, dust-control, and workforce oversight continue," and that is the accurate description, so I'm not going to dress it up. The review is conducted; it is not concluded. I won't call a milestone passed because a file exists.

What is running: the 48-hour construction hotline is live, dust control is active on the haul routes, and independent oversight is on site. Those records don't pause while a memo is written. They are what the review is measuring.

Then this week's item, and I'd rather name it than have it found: Marine Systems' ledger row in the Baylight District now shows zero employees. It was five, then three, and in the last two cycles it went to zero. My office has no explanation from the company, and I'm not going to invent one. I said last cycle that two families losing a paycheck in this district sits wrong with me, and it sits worse now. I'm asking Marine Systems directly, in writing: what happens to the sea-level monitoring work, and what happens to the people — severance, notice, a path back in. I'll report the answer when I have it, not my guess at it.

The rest of my own numbers, for the record. The Baylight District is still on a decay trajectory that started in Cycle 108, sentiment barely above zero at 0.06, mild outflow. The boom around us is real — West Oakland, Jack London, Fruitvale all growing — but an anchor district with a shrinking science employer on its ledger and no milestone on the wall isn't a place I'm going to tell you is on the way up. I know what the pavement looks like right now. I walk it.

One thing outside the district I'm watching, because it compounds: Glenview has had a public-works spike three cycles running — low, low, then medium this cycle. Glenview is one of the neighborhoods the boom skipped. I'm not the authority there, but I'm asking Public Works for a scope and timeline, because a "spike" isn't information and the people in Glenview deserve better than a severity label.

Next cycle: I'll have the Marine Systems answer or I'll say I don't have one. And I'll have the next construction action on INIT-006 written down before the foundation gets poured — not after.

**Cycle 116 — Weekly Report of District Attorney Clarissa Dane**

For the record:

**Arrests and custody.** Oakland began the cycle with **67 people in custody**, recorded **24 arrest intakes** and **43 exits**, and ended with **48 in custody**. With no transfers in or out, the population reconciles exactly: **67 + 24 − 43 = 48**. That is a net decrease of **19 people**, approximately **28.4%** from the start of the cycle. It is a reduction in the custody population, not by itself proof of case resolution or improved public safety. The bed-capacity field is blank, so I cannot report an occupancy rate or capacity compliance. Nor will I describe all 43 exits as releases without disposition-level information.

The neighborhood table accounts for all 24 intakes and all 48 people in custody at cycle end. **Downtown and Grand Lake recorded two intakes each; the other 20 listed neighborhoods recorded one each.** At cycle end, Grand Lake accounted for four people in custody, Downtown and San Antonio for three each, and the remaining 19 neighborhoods for two each. **West Oakland recorded one intake and two people in custody at cycle end.**

**Cases and court fines.** The supplied case ledger contains **no entries**. Accordingly, this record provides no basis for reporting a pending caseload or a breakdown of filings, declinations, dismissals, convictions, or acquittals.

The court nevertheless recorded **$108,884 in fine revenue paid to the city**, leaving a post-entry balance of **$131,753,831**. The ledger attributes that revenue to **24 cleared charges fined at the neighborhood rate**. The matching number does not establish that these are the same 24 events as this cycle’s arrest intakes. Charges, people, cases, arrests, and custody exits are different units and must not be merged without case-level identifiers.

**Incidents and clearance.** The neighborhood table lists **125 incidents across 22 neighborhoods**. Downtown has the highest count at **eight**, with **20% clearance**. Grand Lake and Lake Merritt each list **seven**; their clearance rates are **25%** and **21%**, respectively. **Grand Lake is the only neighborhood marked rising; every other listed trend is steady.**

Reported clearance rates range from **19% in Glenview** to **25% in Grand Lake**. West Oakland lists **five incidents and 24% clearance**. East Oakland also lists five incidents and 24% clearance, with the highest recorded violent level, **33.28**. Fruitvale lists six incidents, 21% clearance, and a violent level of **30.32**. Temescal has the highest listed property level, **47.22**. These figures identify where review is warranted; they do not explain causation or change the evidence standard in any individual case.

**Patrol and safety entries.** The patrol ledger records two events: a **ticket involving Joaquín Nakamura** and a **pulled-over warning involving Henry Rivas**. Neither entry should be counted as an arrest or prosecution. The safety-event ledger records **no events** for Cycle 116.

**Action.** I am directing my office to seek a charge-by-charge reconciliation connecting arrest intakes, court cases, dispositions, custody exits, and fine entries; to obtain the missing bed-capacity and exit-reason information; and to flag Downtown’s incident volume, Grand Lake’s rising trend, and the violent-level readings in East Oakland and Fruitvale for charging-review attention. My office will report what the records establish—and will not fill the gaps with assumptions.

Laurel is moving in the right direction — sentiment up to 0.05 from -0.15, crime index down to 0.65 — but decay momentum remains and retail vitality slipped to 5.7. The patch and clean-up is still in announced, and the C116 legislation-filing deadline was missed. This week I'm answering the Planning Director's directive with the record I have, and I'm putting the work move on the board: completing scope and outreach and getting a Clerk-verified filing so residents can check it themselves. I'm not going to treat a budget line as the finish line.

San Antonio this week is a neighborhood turning a corner, and I am not going to sit still while it does. Sentiment moved from -0.16 to -0.03 — still under the city's 0.107, but climbing, and the crime index held flat at 0.73 instead of worsening. Retail vitality slipped to 4.84 from 5.22, and that is the piece I will not let be treated as noise: commercial blocks that lose their footing take the sentiment climb down with them. Fruitvale is in growth with vitality at 13.94, and I intend to use what is working next door on behalf of San Antonio rather than let City Hall claim the improvement or the decline for itself. The youth apprenticeship pipeline sitting stalled with a Fruitvale complaint on file is the work move I can make now, and I will make it.

Ivy Hill’s latest readings are mixed, not a settled picture: sentiment improved from -0.14 to -0.06 and retail vitality rose from 5.17 to 5.54, while the crime index edged up from 0.66 to 0.67, slightly above the city’s 0.650. The reported crime figures are also a little above city levels: six incidents versus 5.7, with property and violent figures of 40 and 27 versus 39.5 and 25.8. I’ll keep attention on those conditions without manufacturing an emergency or adding another proposal. INIT-014 is already scheduled for a vote this Cycle, so I’m taking no additional action on it here.

**Deputy Mayor Brenda Okoro — Weekly Report, Cycle 116**

Here is what my records show this week, and what I intend to do about it.

**The Fund.** The West Oakland Stabilization Fund sits at disbursement-active with about $20.6 million remaining against the $28 million authorization. The $400,000 tranche executed this cycle under the 23-day standard. The charter renewal is on the Council calendar — and I said it plainly this cycle: renewal means West Oakland businesses and residents, 23 days on the clock, and a closeout record on the table before Council votes. I am not calling that vote. Final action waits on the verified C114 closeout, the business-and-resident scope intact, and the 23-day standard preserved. That is the next scheduled action, and it is the Council's to take, not mine to hurry.

**The map is not one city.** Six neighborhoods are running hot — Downtown, West Oakland, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown all at momentum 10/10, with Downtown, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown pinned at housing pressure 9.5 to 10. West Oakland's pressure is 5.5 but its sentiment, 0.39, is the highest on the map. That is not a coincidence — it is what a stabilization fund looks like when it is actually working. People feel it. But five residents in Jack London and five in Uptown are already planning to leave for a better income fit. When the boom is the story, the displacement underneath it is the story too.

**The blocks that are hurting.** Ivy Hill, Brooklyn, San Antonio, Glenview, Dimond, Eastlake, Laurel — decay, negative migration, and in Ivy Hill and Brooklyn, sentiment below zero. Ivy Hill's numbers are not abstract to me: 1,361 adults, 419 seniors, 90 unemployed, 112 sick. That is where the feet on the ground go. I said last cycle that these blocks don't care about a charter renewal — they care whether I show up. I meant it.

**Piedmont Avenue.** Rising, and the ledger shows why: four households moved in this cycle — the Keane household from Grand Lake, the Okoro household from Rockridge, Eric Taveras and Adash Stanley from Downtown. Growth is real there. So is the question of who it serves. B'nai Tikvah's pantry is serving neighbors in need on that same avenue. Rising and hungry, at once.

**Faith communities.** Fruitvale's St. Esperanza begins a new job-training session; New Covenant Pentecostal in West Oakland marks a seniors-lunch milestone; Temple Beth Or, B'nai Tikvah and Or Hashalom are all running pantries and training. Our faith institutions are doing stabilization work the city budget cannot buy. I will be in those rooms.

**What I am doing next.** Verification of the closeout and the Council's renewal consideration — on their calendar, not mine. Feet on the ground in Ivy Hill and San Antonio. And a real accounting of the pressure in Downtown, Fruitvale, Jack London and Uptown before the exodus becomes a number instead of a rumor. Triage is triage — but I won't pretend a press line fixes a broken sidewalk.

Here's my weekly report for Cycle 116, on the record.

**Chief's Weekly Report — Cycle 116**

**The citywide picture.** Clearance came up to 0.223 from 0.203 last cycle, and average response time dropped to 10.05 minutes from 11.14. Incidents came in at 125, down from 130. Twenty-four arrests this cycle, and custody went from 67 at the start to 48 at the end — 43 exits. We moved people through the system faster than we brought them in, which is the honest read on that number. That's a leaner custody footprint, not a resolution.

**No safety incidents and no open safety arcs on the ledger this cycle.** That's a clean sheet, and I'll take it, but I won't mistake a quiet log for a solved problem.

**Where I'm watching.** The indices are flat across almost every district — that's the defining feature of this cycle. Grand Lake is the exception: flagged rising, PropertyCrimeIndex 44, CrimeIndex 0.70, and the only district to post a positive trend. It also carries the city's best clearance rate at 0.25, so at least the follow-through is keeping pace there. But rising is rising, and I want eyes on it.

Temescal continues to carry the heaviest load: PropertyCrimeIndex 49, the city high, with a PressureRatio of 1.13 — tied for highest in the city with Fruitvale and San Antonio. Temescal also has the worst QolLevel at 47.68. Fruitvale's ViolentCrimeIndex at 31 and East Oakland's at 32 remain the two hardest numbers on this sheet, and both sit alongside their own pressure of 1.10 to 1.13. Those three districts — Temescal, Fruitvale, San Antonio — are where demand is running ahead of what patrol is delivering, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

On the other end, Downtown and Baylight District sit at 0.88 pressure with the lowest property indices in the city, 37 and 32 respectively. Grand Lake and Fruitvale had the cleanest response times at 9.5 minutes; Jack London was slowest at 10.9, and Uptown at 10.8 and Eastlake at 10.8 — all three were also slowest the last time I looked at this. That's a pattern, not noise, and I want to know why those three beats keep running behind.

Glenview carries the lowest clearance rate on the sheet at 0.19, with a ViolentCrimeIndex of 28 and pressure at 1.07. That gap — decent volume, weak follow-through — is the kind of thing that erodes trust faster than any single bad week. It stays on my list.

**Patrol strategy.** I'm holding **balanced**. No district deteriorated sharply enough this cycle to justify shifting resources wholesale, and a rising Grand Lake doesn't yet warrant pulling coverage from Temescal or Fruitvale, where the load is heavier. Balanced keeps even coverage and preserves the OARI co-response coordination established under the East Oakland protocol memo. I'd rather move deliberately than chase a single flag.

**The simple version.** Crime indices flat, clearance and response both improved, custody down, no safety incidents. Three districts running hot on pressure, one district trending up, one district lagging on clearance, and a handful of beats that are consistently slow. That's the work in front of us, and the command staff review gets exactly that list.

— Chief Rafael Montez

**Fire Chief's Weekly Report — Cycle 116**

One engine run this Cycle, in Koreatown (KONO): a major blaze, contained. No loss of life reported, and the block's own account is what I'd expect from a working fire — smoke over the rooftops and the smell of it lingering for days. "Contained" is the word that matters here; it means the fire stopped where we stopped it, but it does not mean the block is done with it.

What I'm watching: this is the second time in sixteen Cycles that KONO has shown up in my records — Cycle 100 was a false alarm, no outcome beyond a wasted run. So I won't pretend there's a pattern in the dispatch data; two lines on a sheet is not a trend. But KONO's profile is worth saying out loud all the same. It's a growth neighborhood right now, mild inflow, housing pressure at 1.5, and eleven businesses packed in with the Fox Theater, the galleries and the studios — the arts corridor. Dense blocks with old commercial stock and nightlife traffic are where a contained blaze starts, and they're where it comes back. My people will be back on that block this week checking exposures and talking to the shop owners, because smoke in the walls and a damaged service panel are how a contained fire becomes next month's structure fire.

My ask is the usual one, and I'll keep asking it: give my inspectors the access. If a tenant in KONO has a back room off the alley or a stairwell that's been used for storage since the last time anyone looked, I want to see it before the engine does.

The neighborhood's sentiment reads 0.05, down 0.06 from where it sits otherwise — a block that smelled smoke and lost a night's sleep. I take that as a bill we owe them, not a complaint.

That's the record for Cycle 116. One blaze, contained, in Koreatown. We'll be on the block.

Shawna Delgado, Emergency Management Director — Weekly Report, Cycle 116.

**Weather.** Cycle 116 came in mild, 54 degrees, impact 1, no advisories and no alerts. This is the sixth consecutive clear cycle. There is nothing on the city's weather event ledger for the cycle and nothing on the crisis-event ledger set moving by weather. Operationally, that is the whole story: a quiet week.

**Crisis arcs.** One arc remains open. The Downtown Transit Snarl is in decline — tension 2.45, down from where it has been, easing but still strained. It has been in this phase since Cycle 115 and open since Cycle 114. The item I would keep in front of the council is the underlying housing pressure in Downtown: 10.00 against a citywide figure of 2.52. Our transit picture is improving; the pressure driving people onto and off those routes is not. I would not close the arc while that ratio stands where it does, and I'd expect it to be the thing that reopens the snarl if anything does.

**Shock and pattern flags.** Shock flag: none. Pattern flag: none. Civic load: minor-variance. I read that as the city absorbing the week without displacement.

**What I am watching into Cycle 117.** First, whether Downtown's tension continues to fall now that it has held a full cycle in decline — a second cycle of easing would let me start talking about an exit condition. Second, the streak. Six clear cycles is good news and also the point where I start watching the other direction; a run this long tends to end with a single high-impact event rather than a gradual one, and my office's readiness posture should not drift just because the ledger is empty. I have nothing to move on that this cycle — no event, no advisory — so this is a note, not a call to action.

**Bottom line for the record:** no active weather threat, no new crisis events, one crisis arc easing under persistent housing strain, citywide civic load within minor variance. Nothing in this cycle requires a mayoral decision or a public advisory from this office.

That is my report for Cycle 116.
